name: Ricardian Equivalence
statement: How a government funds its spending, by taxes now or borrowing to be repaid later, makes no difference to the economy.
meaning: Ricardian equivalence is the proposition that, for a given level of government spending, financing it by current taxes or by borrowing has no effect on aggregate demand, consumption, interest rates, or capital accumulation. Because rational, forward-looking households recognise that a deficit today implies higher taxes tomorrow to service and repay the debt, they save the whole of a deficit-financed tax cut to meet the coming liability. A deficit-financed tax cut therefore does not stimulate spending; in the strong form, households do not treat government bonds as net wealth.
mechanism: The argument rests on the government's intertemporal budget constraint: debt issued today must eventually be repaid through future taxes, so a given spending path is financed one way or another in present-value terms. Forward-looking households internalise this constraint and correctly anticipate the future taxes implied by current deficits, leaving their perceived lifetime wealth unchanged by a bond-financed tax cut, which they save rather than spend. Barro's contribution closed the gap where future taxes fall on later generations: with an operative bequest motive, families act as effectively infinitely-lived dynasties, raising bequests to offset taxes shifted onto their heirs.

examples.text: A household that receives a deficit-financed tax cut, foreseeing the future taxes needed to repay the debt, saves the windfall to meet that liability rather than increasing its consumption.
Because a government bond carries an exactly offsetting future tax, households do not count it as new wealth, the question posed by the title of Barro's 1974 paper.
If taxes are deferred onto future generations, equivalence survives only if parents care about their heirs enough to raise bequests, linking the generations into one long-lived planner.

variants.name: Ricardo's own doubt
variants.text: Ricardo raised the logical possibility in 1820 but doubted it held in practice, believing people take a myopic view of the tax path, so the name is something of a misnomer.

variants.name: Partial equivalence
variants.text: The empirically common finding that households offset only part of a deficit, so equivalence holds approximately at most rather than exactly.

whyItMatters: It is central to debates over whether deficit-financed tax cuts and fiscal stimulus can boost demand, whether government debt crowds out private saving and investment, and whether deficits impose a burden. As a limiting case it defines the benchmark against which the real effects of deficits are measured: to argue that deficits matter is to argue that one of its strong assumptions fails. It thus organises much of the theory of fiscal policy, even for economists who regard it as descriptively false.

working.text: use equivalence as the limiting case against which to measure the real effects of deficits, not as a description of how economies respond.
to judge whether a deficit will matter, ask which of its conditions, infinite horizons, perfect capital markets, lump-sum taxes, no uncertainty, is violated.
anticipate that households offset part but not all of a deficit, since liquidity constraints and finite horizons blunt the full result.

limits: Equivalence relies on strong assumptions widely believed not to hold. It requires infinite horizons or intergenerational altruism through operative bequest motives; if households are finitely-lived and do not fully value their descendants' burdens, it fails. It requires perfect capital markets, so liquidity-constrained households, who spend a tax cut, break it. It assumes lump-sum, non-distortionary taxes and no uncertainty about future income, taxes, or lifespan. Empirically the evidence is mixed and generally finds only partial equivalence, so most economists treat it as a theoretical benchmark rather than an accurate account of how economies respond to deficits.
misreadings: It is not an empirically established fact; the evidence is mixed and at best supports approximate or partial equivalence, so it is best treated as a benchmark rather than a description of reality. The name overstates Ricardo's endorsement: he articulated the logic but explicitly doubted it would hold in practice, and it was Barro, not Ricardo, who revived it as a strong modern proposition. And it does not say deficits never matter in general; it says they are neutral only under conditions that frequently fail.
origin: Traced to David Ricardo, who discussed the idea in his 'Essay on the Funding System' (1820) while doubting its practical force, and revived and formalised by Robert Barro in his 1974 paper 'Are Government Bonds Net Wealth?', with the term popularised by Barro's later work.

sources.text: Barro, 'Are Government Bonds Net Wealth?,' Journal of Political Economy 82(6) (1974): 1095-1117 (Harvard DASH full text). — the modern formalisation and the bequest-motive argument.
